objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Embeddings from `text-embedding-3-large` at full size — 3072 dimensions — must be indexed in an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container. Which vector index types can be used?

options.text: `quantizedFlat` or `diskANN`, both of which allow up to 4096 dimensions
`flat` only, because it is the only type that stores full-precision vectors
Any of `flat`, `quantizedFlat` or `diskANN` — the limit applies to the vector policy, not the index
None; vectors above 2048 dimensions must be reduced before indexing

explanation: `flat` tops out at 505 dimensions, which rules it out immediately. `quantizedFlat` and `diskANN` both accept up to 4096, so a 3072-dimension embedding fits either — the choice between them then comes down to how many vectors the search is scoped to.

whyWrong.B: `flat` is the one type 3072 dimensions will not fit on.
whyWrong.C: The dimension ceiling is a property of the index type; it is exactly what differentiates them here.
whyWrong.D: 4096 is the ceiling for the quantized types, and nothing requires dimensionality reduction at 3072.

docs.title: Vector indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

hint: One of the three types has a dimension limit an order of magnitude below the others.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A container holds about two million indexed vectors and queries search across all of them. Which vector index type gives the lowest latency and RU cost while keeping high accuracy?

options.text: `diskANN`, the most performant above ~50,000 vectors
`quantizedFlat`, since compression beats a graph index
`flat`, since only an exact search can be trusted
No index; a full scan with a `WHERE` filter is cheaper

explanation: The 50,000-vector line is the one to remember: at or below it `quantizedFlat` is the recommendation, above it `diskANN` wins on latency, throughput and RU charge. Both are brute-force versus graph — `quantizedFlat` still scans every quantized vector, which is what stops scaling.

whyWrong.B: `quantizedFlat` is still a brute-force search over compressed vectors; its cost grows with the vector count.
whyWrong.C: `flat` is capped at 505 dimensions and is the most expensive option; exactness is rarely worth it at this scale.
whyWrong.D: Unindexed vector queries cost more RUs, not fewer — that is the whole reason vector indexes exist.

docs.title: Vector indexing policies in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A team adds a `diskANN` index to a test container holding 300 documents with vectors. Queries return correct results but the RU charge is far higher than expected. What explains it?

options.text: `diskANN` needs 1,000 vectors; below that it full-scans
`diskANN` indexes are built lazily until repartitioning
The container is missing the `flat` index it falls back to
RU charges for vector queries do not depend on the index

explanation: Both quantized index types need at least 1,000 vectors before the quantization can be trained accurately. Below that threshold Cosmos DB quietly falls back to a full scan — the results stay correct, which is exactly why the symptom shows up as cost rather than as an error.

whyWrong.B: There is no repartitioning prerequisite for a vector index to be used.
whyWrong.C: Index types are independent; `diskANN` does not fall back to `flat`.
whyWrong.D: RU cost for vector queries drops substantially when an index is actually used.

docs.title: Vector search limitations in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

hint: The results are right and the bill is wrong. That points at a fallback, not a failure.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Complete the container vector policy for 1536-dimension embeddings that should be compared by cosine similarity at full precision.
explanation: `float32` is the full-precision type most embedding models emit; `float16` halves the storage at some accuracy cost. Cosine is both the requested metric and the default. `dimensions` must match the model's output — 1536 here — and is not a limit you pick.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A vector query runs against a container with a `diskANN` index. Run twice against unchanged data, it returns slightly different orderings. Is this a defect?

options.text: No; `diskANN` is approximate and replicas index separately
Yes; the vector policy and index policy have drifted apart
Yes; the index build has not completed on every replica
No; the query is missing an `ORDER BY` to make it stable

explanation: `diskANN` trades guaranteed recall for latency and RU cost, and any replica can serve the query using its own independently built index. If you need identical, exact results every time, `flat` is the only type that promises 100% recall; otherwise `searchListSizeMultiplier` on `VectorDistance` buys recall back at the cost of RUs.

whyWrong.B: Policy drift would surface as the index not being used, not as small ordering differences.
whyWrong.C: The behaviour persists after the build completes; it is inherent to approximate search.
whyWrong.D: The query does have an ordering — approximate search means the candidate set itself can differ.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Which query correctly retrieves the ten most semantically similar documents to a query vector in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?

options.text: `SELECT TOP 10 c.title FROM c ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.v, @q)`
`SELECT c.title FROM c WHERE VectorDistance(c.v, @q) < 0.2`
`SELECT TOP 10 c.title FROM c ORDER BY c.v DESC`
`SELECT c.title, VectorDistance(c.v, @q) AS s FROM c ORDER BY s`

explanation: A vector search is `ORDER BY VectorDistance(...)` with a `TOP N`. The `TOP N` is not cosmetic — without it the engine tries to rank the whole container, and both the RU charge and the latency go up sharply.

whyWrong.B: A raw distance threshold with no ordering or TOP does not give you nearest neighbours, and the cut-off is metric-dependent.
whyWrong.C: Ordering by the vector property itself is meaningless — there is no distance being computed.
whyWrong.D: Missing the `TOP N`, which is the specific thing Microsoft warns about; ordering by the projected alias also does not limit the work.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A container's vector policy specifies 1536 dimensions with cosine distance. The team switches embedding models and now needs 3072 dimensions. What has to happen?

options.text: The policy and index must be dropped and re-added
Update `dimensions`; Cosmos DB reindexes in the background
Nothing; `dimensions` is advisory and any length is accepted
Disable vector search, then re-enable it with new dimensions

explanation: You can add or remove path configurations, but you cannot edit the settings of an existing vector embedding or vector index policy. A dimension change therefore means dropping the policy and index and adding them back — which in practice means a new container and a re-embed of the data.

whyWrong.B: In-place edits to policy settings are not supported; that is the specific limitation being tested.
whyWrong.C: All vectors in a path must share the declared dimensionality.
whyWrong.D: Once vector indexing and search are enabled on a container, they cannot be disabled.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Complete the statements that enable DiskANN vector indexing on an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server database, assuming the extension has already been allowed at server level.

blanks.label: Blank 1 — how the dependency on the `vector` extension is satisfied
Blank 3 — the operator class for cosine distance

explanation: `pg_diskann` depends on `vector`, and `CASCADE` tells PostgreSQL to create that dependency for you rather than failing. The access method is `diskann`, and the operator class must match the distance operator your queries use — `vector_cosine_ops` for `<=>`. Pick the wrong operator class and the planner simply ignores the index.

docs.title: Enable and use DiskANN in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Match each pgvector distance operator to the operator class an index must declare for the planner to use it.
explanation: The operator and the operator class have to agree, or the index is not a candidate and you get a sequential scan — fast enough on a test table, ruinous in production. L2 is Euclidean and uses `<->`; cosine uses `<=>`; inner product uses `<#>`.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: A RAG store on Azure Database for PostgreSQL holds 40 million rows of embeddings. Query recall is acceptable but the index no longer fits comfortably in memory and queries are hitting storage. Which index option addresses this directly?

options.text: Build the index with `product_quantized = true`
Lower `max_neighbors` to 8 to shrink the graph
Set `diskann.l_value_is` to 20 so fewer candidates are fetched
Switch to an `ivfflat` index, which stores no graph structure

explanation: Product quantization compresses the vectors themselves, so far more of the index stays resident and comparisons are done on smaller values. Microsoft recommends turning it on above about a million rows for exactly this reason.

whyWrong.B: Cutting `max_neighbors` well below the recommended 64–96 for a dataset this size trades away recall to save comparatively little.
whyWrong.C: `l_value_is` is a query-time knob: it lowers recall without changing how much memory the index needs.
whyWrong.D: `ivfflat` stores full vectors in lists and does not solve the memory problem; it usually gives worse recall at this scale too.

hint: Two of these change how thoroughly you search. Only one changes how big the thing you are searching is.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: A team wants to index 3072-dimension embeddings in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and finds that their HNSW index creation fails. What is the constraint, and what is the fix?

options.text: HNSW caps at 2,000 dimensions; `pg_diskann` goes to 16,000
HNSW requires the vectors to be normalised first; normalise and retry
HNSW cannot be created on an empty table; insert 1,000 rows and retry
HNSW requires `shared_preload_libraries` to include `vector`; add it and restart

explanation: pgvector's HNSW caps out at 2,000 dimensions, which rules out the full-size large embedding models. DiskANN from v0.6 indexes up to 16,000 dimensions, provided product quantization is turned on — that support is what the quantization unlocks.

whyWrong.B: Normalisation affects which distance metric is meaningful, not whether the index can be built.
whyWrong.C: The 1,000-row minimum is a Cosmos DB rule, not a pgvector one.
whyWrong.D: The extension being allowed and created is a prerequisite generally, but it is not what the dimension limit is about.
